For example, individual sales figures are data, while a monthly sales report that identifies trends provides information that can support decision making.

reference: A relational database organises data into tables containing rows and columns. Each row normally represents a record, while each column represents an attribute of that record. A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key creates a relationship by referring to a primary key in another table. Relational databases also use integrity constraints to maintain reliable data. SQL can then be used to define database structures, retrieve records, update values and combine information from multiple related tables.

reference: Database integrity can be divided into several types. Entity integrity requires a primary key to uniquely identify each record and prevents the key from being null. Referential integrity controls relationships between tables by requiring a foreign key to correspond to an existing primary key, unless a null value is permitted. Domain integrity restricts the values that can be stored in a field. These rules can be implemented using primary keys, foreign keys, unique constraints and check constraints within a relational database management system.

reference: SQL provides different commands for defining and manipulating relational data. Data Definition Language, commonly called DDL, includes commands such as create, alter and drop. Data Manipulation Language, or DML, includes commands such as select, insert, update and delete. SQL joins allow information stored in separate tables to be combined. An inner join returns records with matching values in both tables, while a left join returns every record from the left table together with any corresponding records from the right table.

reference: Organisations can obtain useful data from internal systems, external sources and user-generated content. Internal sources include operational databases, application logs, spreadsheets and data warehouses. External sources may include government datasets, third-party APIs, cloud platforms and publicly available information. User-generated sources can include surveys, reviews, support tickets and application activity. Choosing an appropriate source depends on factors such as relevance, quality, cost, accessibility and legal restrictions. Combining several sources may provide richer information, but it can also create integration and consistency problems.

reference: Data cannot automatically be reused simply because it is available online. Some licences allow broad reuse with attribution, while others restrict commercial activity or require derivative work to use similar licensing conditions. A dataset without a clear licence may still be protected by existing rights. Legal and ethical considerations therefore form an important part of deciding whether external data is appropriate for a project.

reference: Effective data modelling requires more than simply identifying the information that needs to be stored because the appropriate structure depends on how that information will eventually be accessed, updated and analysed. Although the same real-world object can appear in multiple systems, its representation may change substantially according to the purpose of each application. A bookstore, for example, may focus on prices, stock and customer reviews, whereas an academic research system may instead represent publication dates, authors, citations and relationships between different research entities.
